card.hook: Picture a pink Baroque palace, a grey medieval tower and a 1922 parliament building all squashed onto one hilltop, like centuries queuing for the same photo. That's Toompea Castle, and it's a lot of fun to frame.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 20 m east of the subject, and face west toward Toompea Castle. Keep your phone level so the walls and tower stay straight.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole long façade. If you're too close to squeeze the wing in, tap 0.5x. If Tall Hermann is in view, try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the tower and for close shots of the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the walls and tower with the vertical lines so nothing leans.
card.best_time: Aim for sunrise or sunset, when the Estonian flag goes up or comes down on Tall Hermann. The soft early or late light is usually kind to the stonework, but check how it falls on the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Kohtuotsa viewing platform (Kohtu tn 12), at the end of Kohtuotsa Street. Use the front camera, and with the castle's pink Baroque front behind you, try 0.5x to squeeze more in. There's a painted wall nearby that makes a ready-made backdrop.
card.ask_someone: On Lossi plats (Castle Square), you pose in front of the pink façade while your helper stands with Alexander Nevsky Cathedral behind them, and it's worth a quick check on site that you've got the right way round.
card.rules_and_safety: Toompea has uneven surfaces and steep steps, so wear sturdy footwear. Drones are strictly prohibited over Toompea Castle. The castle is the working Parliament, so shoot the outside freely and check the official site and any signs for rules inside.
card.challenge: Take one frame of the wall with nobody in it and one with a person walking past for scale, then pick your winner.
card.good_to_know: Tall Hermann (Pikk Hermann) is 48 metres high, and the flag goes up on it every day at sunrise and comes down at sunset. The medieval walls and towers date largely from the 13th century onwards, and the big Baroque and Neoclassical wing was added after Russia took over in 1710. There's also a 19th-century legend that the heroine Linda built the whole hill boulder by boulder.

selfie_spots.why: From here the castle's pink Baroque front sits behind you, and a painted wall gives a ready-made backdrop for a selfie.

card.hook: Picture a huge, plain hangar sitting right on the water, with old ships tied up along the edge like they're waiting for their turn. That's Seaplane Harbour, and it makes a great photo almost by accident.
card.stand_here: Stand about 460 m north-east of the subject, at Lennusadam (the phone icon on the map), and face south-west. The museum is that way, and from here the hangar shows up as a distant shape across the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the hangar, water and sky together. Then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pull the curves and roofline closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the hangar, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker if the sky is bright, so the building doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives soft light that flatters the hangar and the water. It still works in most daylight, though.
card.selfie_here: Try the quayside in the harbour basin beside the icebreaker Suur Tõll, just outside the museum's main building. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the hangar over your shoulder. No guide describes a selfie here specifically, so check the background fits before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the end of Küti street by the museum's outdoor area, with the icebreaker Suur Tõll in view, while you pose on the quay by the icebreaker; check that the hangar fits in the shot, because we haven't confirmed that framing.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear comfortable shoes, because the hangars and ship decks can be cool and uneven underfoot. The museum itself is ticketed, but you can photograph from the public waterfront; check the official site for current access and ticket details.
card.challenge: Take a few steps along the water's edge between shots and see if you can spot the exact moment the hangar lines up just right.
card.good_to_know: Seaplane Harbour (Lennusadam) is a maritime museum that opened in spring 2012, in a building first put up as a hangar for seaplanes. It stands in the area of Peter the Great's Naval Fortress, and its renovation began in 2010. The best-known exhibit is the 1936 submarine Lembit, and the icebreaker Suur Tõll is another historic vessel here.

card.hook: This pale pink-ish palace practically poses for you: one tidy building, a clear outline and a park around it, so there's almost nothing messy to dodge.
card.stand_here: Stand about 25 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south, with Kadriorg Palace straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which should fit the whole width of the palace from here. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of foreground, and keep the palace central so the edges don't stretch. Try zoom 2x or higher for details like the roofline or windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the roofline with a horizontal line so the palace doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people. At midday you're shooting towards the sun, so the front of the palace can look dark against a bright sky.
card.selfie_here: Try the south shore of the Swan Pond (Luigetiik) in Kadriorg Park, where the palace reflection shows in the water. Use the front camera at 0.5x, then check the screen to see how much of the palace fits over your shoulder, because this spot is approximate.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the forecourt on A. Weizenbergi street, facing the front of the palace, while you stand so the whole facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside of the palace and the gardens can be photographed freely. Inside, photos are allowed but flash is not, to protect the artwork.
card.challenge: Take three shots a few seconds apart while other visitors wander through, then pick the one where the palace has the stage to itself.
card.good_to_know: Peter the Great had the palace built for his wife Catherine. Work began in 1718 and the main building was finished by 1725, and its Estonian and German names both mean "Catherine's valley". Restoration began in 1991 and it reopened in 2000. It now houses the Kadriorg Art Museum, with foreign art from the 16th to the 20th century, while Estonian art is at Kumu, nearby in the same park.

card.hook: Most people shoot Viru Gate from the street and end up with a stranger's elbow in the corner. Climb a few steps instead and the two red-roofed towers rise right over the crowd.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m south of the subject, in Musumägi (the phone icon on the map), and face north. It's up the short staircase from the gate area, so you look down at the towers from a slight angle.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get both towers and a bit of street. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the red roofs and cut down the crowds. Use 0.5x only if you step closer and want the full height of the towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line both towers up on one vertical line, then tap the towers and slide darker a little so the sky stays blue and the roofs stay red.
card.best_time: Go when the park and gate area are quieter. The light changes through the seasons, so check how it looks on the day. The flower stalls are seasonal and busy in peak season, so expect people in the bottom of your frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the Musumägi staircase: use the front camera and hold it a little high so the gate sits behind you and the crowds stay out of the frame. For colour, switch to the flower stalls at the foot of the towers and use 0.5x to fit the twin roofs over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the park side beside the gate, where the ivy looks best, while you stand in front of the flower stalls at the foot of the towers.
card.rules_and_safety: The towers can't be entered, so take your photos from outside. Musumägi has some uneven steps, so watch your footing while you hold your phone up.
card.challenge: Take one shot from the park side and one from the flower-shop side, then see which one makes you smile more.
card.good_to_know: Viru Gate is a pair of round towers with red conical roofs. The flower stalls at the base add colour, and the ivy looks best from the park side. Guides call the Musumägi view a quieter, elevated alternative and some say it's an underrated photo spot.

card.hook: Telliskivi's front door is a brick gateway with a loud mural beside it, and nearly everyone stops to photograph it. Join them, it's a great way to start your visit.
card.stand_here: Stand at the main entrance gate at Telliskivi 60a (Telliskivi Loomelinnak). The phone icon on the map is right at the gate, so there's no extra walk. Face the courtyard so the brick gateway frames it, with the mural on one side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the gateway, mural and courtyard in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Try 2x to pick out a patch of mural or brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep your phone level so the walls stay straight, then tap the brightest part of the mural and slide to a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the courtyard is lit and the mural colours really show.
card.selfie_here: Try the alley between the old textile factory and the Fotografiska building on the east side of the complex, where the walls are packed with murals. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn your back to the wall so the murals fill the space behind your shoulder. You can also look for the hipster-and-skeleton selfie stencil in the heart of Telliskivi, a mural that's already about selfies.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back across from the brick smokestack with the giant blue bird, so the entrance and the complex both fit in your picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear sturdy shoes for uneven cobbles and outdoor yards. Fotografiska may have its own opening times, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the gateway from different heights and distances, then pick the one where the mural and brick look best together.
card.good_to_know: Telliskivi Creative City is a district of converted industrial buildings. Murals get repainted often, so yours may not match older photos online, but the gateway, brick and courtyard will still look good. For a second view, Fotografiska Tallinn is recommended for an elevated look over the rust-red roofs toward the medieval skyline.

card.hook: Five onion domes rise over Toompea hill, so you can't really lose this cathedral. The fun part is getting all of them in one shot without the top getting chopped off.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 20 m west of the cathedral, and face east. The whole building and its domes should be in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to take in the whole cathedral. If the domes are getting cut off at the top, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close shots of the domes, crosses and decoration.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the cathedral, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the pale walls and sky keep their detail and the gilded crosses don't blow out.
card.best_time: Mid to late afternoon is a good bet, because the sun should be behind you and light up the side you're facing. Early morning tends to be quieter if you want fewer people in the shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to Lossi plats (Castle Square) on Toompea Hill, by Toompea Castle. Face the castle's facade with the cathedral directly behind you, use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it), and check the cathedral is really over your shoulder before you snap.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the square in front of the cathedral's facade, and ask the photographer to step back toward Toompea Castle so the full facade and domes fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship, so dress modestly if you go inside. Sources disagree on photos indoors, so check the posted signs. The Toompea streets are old cobblestones, so wear comfortable shoes.
card.challenge: Get all five domes in one shot with a little sky above the highest one, then zoom in for a close-up of a gilded cross.
card.good_to_know: This is the largest cupola church in Tallinn. It was built between 1894 and 1900, when Estonia was part of the Russian Empire, in the Russian Revival style by Mikhail Preobrazhensky. Inside are eleven bells cast in Saint Petersburg, and the biggest weighs about 16 tons.

card.hook: You walk up, the city opens out below you, and suddenly every phone in sight is out. Good news: you only need a few minutes here to leave with a handful of great frames.
card.stand_here: Stand about 15 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west to take a first frame of Kohtuotsa viewing platform. Then walk up to the platform edge for the view itself.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the platform and the whole view in, then try 1x for a more natural look. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out far-away details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the horizon up with one of them, and keep a little of the platform edge in the corner so it feels like a real place.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day the light is soft and flattering, and a clear day gives you the longest view. Go early in the morning for fewer people, because the terrace fills quickly on summer afternoons.
card.selfie_here: Try the pale pink painted wall of the building right next to the platform (Kohtu tn 12). Use the front camera, stand in front of the wall and let the Old Town rooftops sit behind you. Guides say it's the platform's best-known photo backdrop, and going early or at sunrise helps you skip the queue.
card.rules_and_safety: The path up to the platform can be uneven in places (cobbles, rocks, tree roots), though it's described as safe and wide. The wall is private property and has been repainted more than once, so it may not match older photos.
card.challenge: Take the same view at 0.5x and again at 2x, then pick a winner. Bonus points if you can't decide.
card.good_to_know: Kohtuotsa is a lookout in Tallinn, and the view over the city is the reason to come. It's easy to fit into a walk. People come and go quickly here, so if someone's in your way, a short wait usually clears it.

card.hook: Picture a long, slim spire peeking up from behind a row of stone towers, like it's trying to see over the garden wall. That's the postcard view of St. Olaf's, and you get it from the Toompea cliff edge.
card.stand_here: Stand about 460 m south-west of the subject, on Patkuli vaateplatvorm (the phone icon on the map), and face north-east. You'll be looking over the Old Town walls and towers, with the spire rising behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the walls, towers and spire all fit. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the spire closer. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the spire tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the spire on one of the vertical lines so it stands up straight, then tap the spire and slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually calmer, and the light is softer. Patkuli and Kohtuotsa can get crowded, so go early if you want the viewpoint to yourself.
card.selfie_here: At Patkuli, face the city walls and towers and use the front camera with the spire behind you. Try 0.5x if your front camera has it, and keep the spire over your shoulder. For a different backdrop, the rosy wall with the words "The times we had" at the Kohtuotsa viewpoint also has the spire rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower climb is steep and the top is windy, so hold onto your hat. It's paid and may be closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the spire standing perfectly on a gridline, with the towers filling the bottom half and you grinning in the corner?
card.good_to_know: St. Olaf's is the tallest church building in Estonia, and its spire stands at about 124 metres. The first written mention is from 1267. From 1944 until 1991 the Soviet KGB used the spire as a radio tower and lookout. A local legend says the builder, a stranger named Olev, fell from the tower when the townspeople shouted his name.

selfie_research.notes: The ask-someone spot is the author's favourite view of St. Olaf's, not a stated photo point for passers-by, and the page gives no exact standing place, so check it on arrival. The two selfie spots are viewpoints near the church rather than on its grounds, and the St. Olaf's tower is open only seasonally (April to October per most sources). The tower's platform is sometimes described as about 60 m high, which places it closer to the viewpoints. No page states any selfie stick or tripod rules, so the rules list is empty.

card.hook: Tallinn's Town Hall is a bit crooked, and nobody minds. It grew in stages over several centuries, and the wonky charm is half the reason you'll want the photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Town Hall Square about 60 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The Town Hall and its tower sit straight ahead.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole Town Hall and tower. Try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for the spire and the Old Thomas weather vane, and 0.5x only from back here for the whole square, because up close it stretches the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the spire stands straight, and keep your phone upright and level.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the square. In the evening, try night mode and hold your phone steady against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Try the corner between the coloured guild-style houses beside the Troika restaurant, or the start of Mündi Street facing back toward the square. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and check on the spot that the Town Hall really is over your shoulder before you snap.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the southeast corner of the square and shoot toward the Town Hall while you stand in front of the building, so the spire frames the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is an open public space, but the Town Hall itself works as a museum and concert venue, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Get the spire perfectly straight on a gridline with Old Thomas still visible at the top, before the crowd wanders through.
card.good_to_know: This is the oldest town hall in the Baltic Sea region and Scandinavia, and the last surviving Gothic town hall in Northern Europe. The slim tower rises 64 metres, and the weather vane Old Thomas (Vana Toomas) has been a symbol of Tallinn since 1530. The Old Town has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1997.

selfie_spots.name: Town Hall Square (Raekoja plats), between the three or four coloured houses beside the Troika restaurant
selfie_spots.detail: in the square, in the corner between the coloured guild-style houses with the Troika restaurant in the middle
selfie_spots.why: Two blogs name this as their favourite picturesque corner of the square, but none of them says the Town Hall is behind the visitor, so check the framing on site.

card.hook: Most museums keep the good stuff indoors, but Kumu wears it on the outside. Its curved wall of pale limestone and glass borrows the sky and trees of Kadriorg Park, so no two photos look quite the same.
card.stand_here: Stand about 85 m south-east of the subject, at KUMU (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. You'll see the curved front with the sky and park reflected in the glass.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole curved front in from fairly close. Then try 1x from further back for a calmer, less stretched look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a close-up of the stone and glass.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the glass part of the front, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky reflections keep their detail and the pale stone doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sky has some cloud or colour, because the glass shows it off. Soft daylight is kinder to the pale stone than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: If you go inside, take your selfie in the open-air courtyard with the curved limestone walls behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the walls sweep around over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and stand in front of the big 'KUNST' letters at the park-side entrance, so they can fit you and the building into one shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash isn't allowed, and some temporary exhibitions ban photography, so check the official site before you go. The courtyard needs a museum ticket.
card.challenge: Take your full-front photo first, then walk closer and find a tree reflection in the glass or the join between stone and glass.
card.good_to_know: Kumu is Tallinn's art museum, set in Kadriorg Park. The curved front is made of pale limestone and glass, and visitor guides say it looks different from each angle. The courtyard has bronze and modern sculptures, and it's open on Mondays only in summer, through 30 September.

selfie_spots.why: The courtyard is framed by the building's curved limestone walls, so those walls can form the backdrop behind you.

The Art Museum of Estonia page also says commercial photography in the atrium and courtyard requires a fee and prior agreement.

card.hook: Picture a big round stone tower rising above green terraces, like a castle in a storybook. That's Kiek in de Kök, and the lawn in front is the best seat in the house.
card.stand_here: Stand in Taani Kuninga aed, about 85 m north of the subject (the tower), on the edge nearest the tower. Face south and the round tower rises above the green terraces.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the terraced lawn and the whole tower in one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer view, and 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines and keep your phone level so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the stonework. You're shooting towards the south, so check where the sun is before you pick your spot.
card.selfie_here: Head into the Danish King's Garden and pose beside the hooded monk statues, which are a popular photo subject. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low to fit in the walls and towers. For a different backdrop, stand at the base of the tower facing the stone walls with cannonballs stuck in them.
card.rules_and_safety: The garden is an open public park, but the museum and tower interior are ticketed, so check the official site before you go. Inside, the stone floors are uneven and can be slippery if it has rained, so wear real shoes.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the lawn filling the bottom third, then step in for a tight tower shot, and see which one you'd frame.
card.good_to_know: Kiek in de Kök is a round tower in Tallinn, right by the Danish King's Garden. The garden is also where you reach the museum entrance, so most visitors walk through it before going in. You'll find street statues there too, which make fun foreground subjects for a second shot.

selfie_spots.name: Danish King's Garden, among the monk statues
selfie_spots.detail: on the terraced garden against the city wall, standing beside the hooded monk sculptures
selfie_spots.why: The garden hugs the medieval fortifications with towers rising on either side, and the monk sculptures are a popular photo subject, especially in early morning or late afternoon light.

card.hook: Picture this: you've climbed up to a quiet terrace, and the whole Old Town of Tallinn is spread out right in front of you. No hunting for an angle, no dodging parked cars. Just one spot, one view, and a sky that keeps changing.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 25 m north of the subject, and face south. From there you can fit the platform and the view into one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view, then go to 0.5x if you want to squeeze in more of the scene. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one detail in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, depending on whether the sky or the town below looks more interesting.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can make the view look flat and hazy.
card.selfie_here: Head to the terrace at the top of the Patkuli viewing platform and stand with the Old Town in view below and behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the city over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: One reviewer found the stairs very slippery with icy ground in winter, so hold the rail. Check local signage for access and any rules.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the same view, shifting just a step each time, then see which one lines everything up best.
card.good_to_know: Patkuli viewing platform is a lookout in Tallinn. It's a fixed, easy-to-find spot, which makes a quick phone stop simple. Give your phone lens a quick wipe on a clean sleeve first, because smudges show up most on hazy, bright views.

selfie_spots.name: Terrace on the Patkuli viewing platform
selfie_spots.detail: the terrace at the top of the platform, standing with the Old Town in view below and behind you
selfie_spots.why: A Tripadvisor reviewer calls this terrace a spot that is just perfect for photos of the city, with the Old Town right in front of and beneath the viewer.

sources.title: Absolutely best Tallin viewpoint - Review of Patkuli Viewing Platform - Tripadvisor

selfie_research.safety: A Google reviewer reported the stairs were very slippery with icy ground in winter and advised holding the rail.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a standing spot for a passer-by to photograph a visitor with the whole platform in frame, so ask_someone_spot is null. Several pages (Teamthomas Travels, Wanderlog) describe a graffiti wall reading 'Tallinn' as a selfie spot, but Teamthomas gives that wall's address as Kohtu tn 12, which is Kohtuotsa, a separate platform about 200 m away; I left it out because no page clearly places it at Patkuli. No page I found states rules on selfie sticks or tripods; reviewers only complain about selfie sticks being common in crowds. The platform's coordinates in the question match the Wikimedia Commons map location for Patkul viewing platform.

card.hook: Walls on both sides of a narrow lane are a gift. They act like arrows and point everyone's eye straight to the far end of your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand about 25 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east towards St. Catherine's Passage. It's only a short walk, so you can take a few frames, step closer and take a few more.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit in the whole scene, then switch to 1x for a more natural look. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out a detail like a door, an arch or a surface texture.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the walls and doorframes with the vertical lines, so the lane doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Early morning or a quiet moment outside the busiest hours should give you the lane with fewer people in it. An overcast day also tends to give nice, even light.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the Müürivahe Street end of St. Catherine's Passage, then turn so the passage is behind you and you're looking back toward Vene Street. Use the front camera and hold it at arm's length. A guide says the stone arches stack up from this end, so your selfie should look dense and properly medieval.
card.rules_and_safety: Check local signs for any access restrictions before you go in. The space is tight, so move slowly and don't block the way for people passing.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, then one close-up of a single detail, and see if a friend can guess where the close-up is from.
card.good_to_know: St. Catherine's Passage is a lane with walls on both sides, which makes it great for strong lines. A guide describes its stone arches as a medieval highlight. The Müürivahe Street end and the Vene Street end give you two different views.

selfie_spots.name: Far east end of St. Catherine's Passage, near Müürivahe Street
selfie_spots.detail: Stand at the Müürivahe Street end of the passage with the passage behind you, looking back toward Vene Street
selfie_spots.why: A guide recommends this end for a zoomed-in view that stacks the stone arches, which should make a selfie with the lane behind look dense and medieval.

sources.title: St. Catherine's Passage Guide: Tallinn's Medieval Alley

selfie_research.notes: Spot 1 comes from a photographer's compression-shot tip, not a page about selfies; the 'visitor standing with the passage behind' placement is my inference from that tip. Only one selfie spot had page support; I found no page naming a second. No page gave a spot for a passer-by to photograph a visitor with the whole passage in frame, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page stated selfie stick or tripod rules. Sources conflict on hours: one says the alley is open 24/7, while trip.com lists entry hours of about 10:00–16:00 and advises checking for winter changes. Best light is also described differently: some pages say the first hours after sunrise, others say after dark when the street lights come on.

card.hook: Fat Margaret looks like it could win an arm-wrestle with the rest of Tallinn's Old Town. It's squat, round and very solid, and it looks best from the park side, not the harbour side it was built to impress.
card.stand_here: Stand in Margareeta aed, about 50 m south-east of the subject, and face north-west. The tower is right ahead of you, rising out of the lawn and trees.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole round tower in. If it's too big for the frame, drop to 0.5x. Try 2x to 5x to pick out the stonework and the upper wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep your phone upright so the walls stay straight, and put the tower on one of the vertical lines with the lawn filling the bottom.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the stonework more than harsh midday sun. If the sky is bright, tap the stonework and slide the picture a little darker so the stone keeps its colour.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the Fat Margaret rooftop terrace, the open-air roof at the top of the tower, which you reach by lift or stairs. A guide calls it a perfect place for photos and selfies, with harbour and Old Town views. Use the front camera and try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the view. You'll be standing on the tower, so it won't be behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Pikk street, where it runs up to the Great Coastal Gate beside the tower, to take a quick photo of you.
card.rules_and_safety: The roof terrace can be used for photos in winter only if there's no severe ice hazard. The park and the lane are free to stand in, but the tower is a museum, so check the official site before you go inside.
card.challenge: Get the whole round tower in one frame with the lawn below it and the walls dead straight, then take one more with a little space above the top.
card.good_to_know: Fat Margaret was built between 1511 and 1530 as part of the rebuilt gate defences. The walls are about 25 metres across, 20 metres high and up to 5 metres thick, which is where the name comes from. It has been a gunpowder and weapons store and a prison, and since the 1978 to 1981 reconstruction it has housed the Estonian Maritime Museum.

selfie_spots.detail: on the open-air roof terrace at the top of the tower, reached by lift or stairs
selfie_spots.why: A guide calls the tower-top viewing platform the perfect place for photos and selfies, with harbour and Old Town views, though the pages do not say the tower stands behind the visitor.

card.hook: Up on the Kohtuotsa terrace, a tall spire rises out of the Old Town roofs and Toompea hill wraps around it. It's the church doing its best to be the star of your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kohtuotsa, about 180 m north of the subject (the phone icon on the map), and face south. The spire and the Old Town roofs will be right below you.
card.zoom: Zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone, to pick out the spire and the roofs around it. Drop to zoom 1x if you'd rather have Toompea and more of the Old Town in the picture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the spire on one of the vertical lines, and keep the phone level so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the terrace.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and try zoom 0.5x so more of the scene squeezes in beside you. Hold the phone a little higher than usual and keep your arm steady.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the platform and ask a passer-by to frame you with the church in view across the rooftops, on the right side of the panorama, and keep the church in the frame rather than trying to fit it behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The terrace is public but popular, so expect to share the railing at busy times. The church is a museum and concert hall, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Can you get the spire sitting neatly on a gridline, with the tower dead straight and not a single leaning roof?
card.good_to_know: St Nicholas' Church (Niguliste kirik) was built around 1230-1275 by Westphalian merchants and named for Saint Nicholas, the patron of fishermen and sailors. The tower is now 105 metres high, with a Baroque spire from the late 17th century. After bomb damage in 1944 it was restored over many years, and today it's the Niguliste Museum and a concert hall, home to Bernt Notke's Danse Macabre.

ask_someone_spot.name: Kohtuotsa viewing platform (Kohtu tn 12, Toompea Hill)
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand at the platform overlooking the Old Town and ask the passer-by to frame you with St. Nicholas' Church in view across the rooftops, which is where it appears on the right side of the panorama. Keep the church in the frame rather than trying to fit it behind you.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where the visitor stands with St. Nicholas' Church directly behind them, so no selfie spot is given. The Kohtuotsa suggestion is my inference from pages that show the church visible from that viewpoint (a Getty photo captioned 'view from Kohtuotsa viewpoint' and a Tripadvisor review placing the church in the panorama); no page describes a photo taken of a visitor there. Pages that mention photo angles for the church itself (Locationscout, Trip.com) give no named spot. No page states selfie-stick or tripod rules for this site. The 'no photography allowed' review on Tripadvisor refers to the separate St. Nicholas' Orthodox Church on Toompea, not to this Niguliste church/museum, so I did not use it as a rule. Coordinates given (59.43588, 24.74271) are close to the church, which the Wikimedia photo pages place at about 59.435 N, 24.744 E.

card.hook: Most of Tallinn's Old Town is a jumble of rooftops, but here you get one tall tower and a clean white front, and nothing in the way. Toomkirik is the oldest church in Tallinn, and it looks great on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand about 65 m south of the subject, on Toom-Kooli (the phone icon on the map), and face north. You'll be looking straight at the tower and the white facade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front. If you're too close to fit it all in, drop to 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tower and spire.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands up straight, then tap the white facade and nudge the picture a touch darker so the walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before about 9:00 in summer. The square is quiet and the light comes from the east, so you can frame the whole front without people wandering through.
card.selfie_here: Try the Bishop's Garden Viewing Platform on Toompea, an open panorama spot that's best at sunset. Use the front camera, or 0.5x to fit more in. Check the framing when you get there, because the cathedral may only just show behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to stand on the small square in front of the cathedral facade, far enough back to get the tower and the whole front, with you posing in front.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside are fine for personal use, but flash is discouraged near the older wooden artifacts and paintings. Photography is strictly prohibited during church services. For the inside or the tower, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots from three different distances, and see if you can keep the tower perfectly upright in all of them.
card.good_to_know: St Mary's Cathedral was founded in the 13th century as a Catholic cathedral and is the oldest church in mainland Estonia. It became Lutheran in 1561. The exterior dates from the 15th century, and the baroque spire was added in 1778-79.

card.hook: Picture a street called Long Leg, running away from you like it has somewhere to be. That's Pikk jalg, and it's a great pick when you want a photo with the city's character rather than just one landmark.
card.stand_here: Stand about 10 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Let the street run away from you down the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the street. If you can't fit the whole scene in, tap 0.5x. Save 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close-up details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the main line of the street along one of the vertical lines, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter, so you'll get fewer people in your frame. Evening gives a softer mood, and night mode helps once it gets dark.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the lower stretch of the cobbled street on Pikk jalg, below the Long Leg Gate Tower, and face down the slope so the tower is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in the arched gateway over your shoulder, and hold the phone a little higher than usual.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand further down the slope on Pikk jalg and shoot up the street, so the gate tower fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cobbles can get very slippery in winter, so watch your step while you back up for a shot. Access rules here aren't confirmed, so follow any local signs and be kind to residents and other people on the street.
card.challenge: Take one frame with the street leading the eye, then wait for a single walker to stroll into it and show how big the street really is.
card.good_to_know: The name Pikk jalg means 'Long Leg', which is a fun thing to put in your caption. The street also has a steep slope. A short walk along it gives you several different pictures, because the view changes every few steps.

selfie_research.notes: No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules, so the rules list is empty. The selfie spot on Pikk jalg is my inference from the gate tower's position; the sources describe the view back toward the lower town and do not describe a selfie. The Patkuli viewing platform tip describes a photographer's position, but that platform is not on Pikk jalg, so I left it out. card.hook: Imagine a row of red-roofed towers standing in line like they're waiting for a bus, with a patch of grass in front. That's the Tallinn City Wall view everyone wants, and it's easier to get than you'd think.
card.stand_here: Stand about 620 m north of the subject, in Tornide väljak (the phone icon on the map), and face south. You're in the little grassy park at the foot of the wall, looking at the towers lined up in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole row of towers and the grass in front. Try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a single tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the wall up along a horizontal line, and let some grass fill the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when guides say the light is best here. Take a few shots from the park first, then wander along the wall for a tighter one.
card.selfie_here: Try Müürivahe Street, at the entrance to the Hellemann Tower walkway, where the tower rises over the lane. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low so the wall fills the frame over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at ground level in the Tornide väljak park so the whole line of towers fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine on the wall, but follow any signs inside tower exhibitions or private areas. Tower stairs are steep and uneven, and the wall-walk towers are ticketed with varying times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Keep your phone perfectly upright and see if you can make every tower stand up straight, with no leaning!
card.good_to_know: Tallinn's medieval wall is one of the reasons the Old Town is a World Heritage Site. Margaret Sambiria ordered the first wall in 1265, and it was under 5 metres tall and about 1.5 metres thick at the base. In the fourteenth century, townspeople had to turn out for guard duty in their armour.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found states a selfie stick or tripod rule for the city wall. Tower entry is ticketed and some towers close on certain days, so check schedules before visiting. The Breathe Baby sign is at Danish King's Garden, and one source calls it a spot to pose with the walls behind; another guide says the sign is painted over in places, so the exact sign may have changed. The Müürivahe spot is inferred from guides saying the towers rise over that lane, not from a page naming a selfie pose there. Ask-someone spot relies on guides calling the park the best ground-level angle for the row of towers; I did not find a page naming a specific standing point within the park.
